lines: I remember the page turning back from a <shake>very bad ending</shake>.
Your face was one of the first things I could <pulse>recognize again</pulse>.
You brought me home when I could not remember what home meant.
I remember the weakness, the medicine, and you refusing to leave.
The cure returned me piece by piece. You waited for every one.
I can read my own notes again because you took that risk.
Some mornings still feel borrowed, and I know who made that possible.
I owe you thanks that no trade discount could properly express.
The village sounds different now that I can understand it again.
You saw a person where the curse had hidden one.
I remember your voice reaching me before the rest of the world did.
Every ordinary day since then feels like a gift I nearly lost.
I had forgotten the smell of paper and clean rain. You gave both back to me.
You stayed close through something most people would have fled.
I am alive, myself, and able to say your name. That is no small thing.
I wrote down what you did so gratitude would not depend on memory alone.
The cure hurt, but waking to a familiar face made it bearable.
I still have bad nights. The mornings belong partly to you.
No ceremony. Just know that I remember your kindness clearly.
If you ever doubt you helped this village, look at me.
The chapter is damaged, but your name survived in the <italic>margin</italic>.
I remember fragments of weakness, gold, a bitter drink, and you waiting.
Your face stayed clear even when the room around it did not.
I know you helped me. The order of events still slips away.
Some memories returned with names. Others came back as sounds.
I recall a cold floor and your hands holding the cup steady.
The days before the cure feel shuffled whenever I reach for them.
I found your name in my own notes before I remembered writing it.
There is a gap where the worst part should be. I may be grateful for that.
I know this village again, though some corners still feel new.
You tell me I spoke during the cure. I remember none of it.
I can place the bell, the lectern, and you. The rest arrives slowly.
The memory breaks whenever I reach the moment I changed back.
I remember being afraid of the light and then wanting more of it.
My hands know these shelves better than my mind does some days.
I have written down what others told me, but it does not feel like mine yet.
Your kindness is a fact even where my memory is uncertain.
I may ask what happened more than once. Please do not mistake that for doubt.
Pieces keep returning at strange times. Your voice is in several of them.
The account is incomplete, but I know who helped bring me through it.
I remember you. Please let me choose how close we stand.
I know you helped, and I still need room to breathe around the memory.
The cure left echoes behind. Sudden movement wakes them.
I am grateful. I am also frightened, and both things can be true.
Do not touch me without warning. The worst memories begin that way.
Your face belongs to the rescue, but it also belongs to that terrible room.
I trust what you did more than I trust my body to stay calm.
Please keep your voice low. Some sounds still take me back.
I remember the cure clearly enough to know I never want another.
You saved me. Give me time to feel safe while knowing that.
I can speak about it, but not with you blocking the door.
The smell of brewing still turns my stomach.
I wake with my hands shaking and have to name everything in the room.
I know where I am now. Sometimes fear takes longer to learn it.
Let us keep this conversation short today.
I do not blame you for the pain. I cannot pretend it never happened.
Stand by the window, please. Open space helps.
I will thank you without making myself relive every detail.
Recovery has been slower than the cure itself.
I am here, and that is enough for this moment.
